title: GPU runtime profiling deep dive - Arcadia Health
summary: Deep dive on GPU runtime profiling between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM approaches, CUDA graphing, kernel selection impacts, KV cache behavior with long sequences, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and Arcadia's VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run targeted benchmarks and share perf sheets; Redwood to provide kernel-level guidance and a pilot plan for on-prem cluster tests.
topics: KV cache policies and prefix caching
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time, this is Jordan and with me is Maya, our runtime SE, and Liam. We're here to walk through the GPU runtime profiling you asked for — kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM and vLLM comparisons, CUDA graphs, KV cache behavior, and any constraints you have for on-prem/VPC deploys.
[00:00:30] Evan (Arcadia): Thanks, Jordan. We're mostly worried about p50->p99 tail latency for a mix of short and long prompts, and also data residency. Our infra team wants to know if Dedicated or Private will map better for us.
[00:00:52] Maya (Redwood SE): Cool. Quick agenda: we'll start with the high-level perf differences we see between TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) and vLLM, then show kernel selection effects, talk CUDA graph capture/warm-up, discuss KV/prefix cache, batching, and quantization notes. We'll call out ops that usually dominate.
[00:01:20] Priya (Arcadia): Also security: SOC2, KMS, SSO — Marcus will handle those questions.
[00:01:30] Marcus (Arcadia): Yep. We'll flag anything that requires HSM or private KMS.
[00:01:36] Maya: Understood.
[00:01:50] Maya: So on TRT-LLM side we generally see much higher token throughput for long sequences once the kernels are specialized — the graph compile and kernel selection is more aggressive. But the tradeoff is the cold-start: TensorRT graph compilation and CUDA graph capture can add tens of seconds for unseen shapes.
[00:02:15] Dr. Sara (Arcadia): When you say "shapes" do you mean sequence length and batch size combinations?
[00:02:20] Maya: Exactly, sequence length, beam width, and sometimes kv cache length. If you have a lot of unique short sequences, vLLM's dynamic scheduling and continuous batching can outperform TRT-LLM because there's less compile overhead.
[00:02:40] Jordan: One thing we saw in your initial perf sheet — thanks for that — is a heavy mix: 60% short chat prompts (~32 tokens), 30% medium (~128 tokens), 10% long (~1024+). That mix makes caching and batching policy critical.
[00:03:00] Evan: Yep that's accurate. We also have a subset of asynchronous background tasks that run long seqs for summarization.
[00:03:10] Maya: For KV cache, TRT-LLM benefits from persistent KV layouts in GPU memory when you pin the same model instance. That reduces per-token memcopy. vLLM's KV cache is more flexible with sub-batching, but it can have overhead when migrating KV between contexts.
[00:03:34] Priya: We plan to deploy in our VPC with private nodes. Does that change any of the kernel behavior?
[00:03:42] Liam: Not kernel behavior, but it affects orchestration — e.g., keeping model instances warm on pinned GPUs vs. ephemeral containers. For on-prem you usually want pinned model pods to amortize CUDA graph and kernel autogen costs.
[00:04:05] Jordan: Quick demo screen share: (link to perf-results.xlsx). On slide 3 we profiled GPT-style 7B variant. TRT-LLM with per-shape kernels gave ~3.4x tokens/sec for long sequences vs vLLM, but for short sequences vLLM was ~1.2x better in p50 latency.
[00:04:35] Dr. Sara: Those numbers look promising, but what about p99? We care about the tail.
[00:04:41] Maya: p99 for TRT-LLM depends heavily on cache hit rates and graph warm state. If you have a warm model pinned with a captured CUDA graph for the common seq length, p99 can be tight. But if you constantly hit new shapes, TRT-LLM p99 balloons because the runtime triggers kernel selection/compilation.
[00:04:59] Evan: How long does that compilation take typically?
[00:05:04] Maya: It varies — small kernels a few hundred ms, large fused kernels or attention kernels can take multiple seconds. The biggest hit is first-time tens-of-seconds on massive ops when we JIT certain primitives or when TensorRT needs to reoptimize for mixed precision.
[00:05:25] Marcus: That could be problematic for our surgeon-facing assistants where latency spikes are unacceptable.
[00:05:30] Jordan: That's where batching and warm pools come in. You can allocate a small pool of pinned instances for low-latency paths, and route background or lower-priority requests to burst capacity.
[00:05:45] Maya: On batching: vLLM continuous batching is great for maximizing throughput at the cost of a small additional latency smoothing; TRT-LLM can use dynamic batching but you lose the kernel specialization advantages if you over-multiplex shapes.
[00:06:05] Priya: Any tips on batch size heuristics? We saw docs suggesting batch=8 for 7B on A100, but that's old.
[00:06:12] Maya: Heuristics: pick a target latency SLO (e.g., p50 100ms) and optimize batching for that. We run per-route autoscaling and batching policies — small interactive routes keep batch sizes 1-4, background routes 16-64. Also consider micro-batching combined with prefix caching.
[00:06:34] Evan: What's your take on INT8 quantization — quality vs perf?
[00:06:39] Maya: INT8 can give 2-4x throughput depending on kernel support, but you need calibration and sometimes per-layer tuning. TensorRT has stronger INT8 kernels but quantization quality can regress on instruction-heavy prompts; we recommend running evals on your prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can suggest layers to keep in FP16 while quantizing others.
[00:07:05] Jordan: We actually ran an internal eval: on our doc summarization dataset, INT8 dropped Rouge-L by ~1.8 points for that 7B — acceptable for some pipelines, not for clinical summaries.
[00:07:20] Dr. Sara: For clinical summaries we need near-zero regression. So quantization might be limited to non-critical paths.
[00:07:27] Maya: Totally understood. Keep critical flows in FP16 or FP32. We can apply mixed quantization — FP16 for attention, INT8 for feedforward — it's model dependent.
[00:07:40] [00:07:40] Priya: About CUDA graphs: can you explain warm-up and how to avoid runtime captures during traffic spikes?
[00:07:49] Maya: Sure. CUDA graphs capture a sequence of GPU ops for a specific shape and then replay them with low overhead. The capture itself is expensive. Best practice: pre-capture graphs for your common shapes during instance startup or during quiet windows. Also maintain a small warm pool per region so a cold request doesn't block capture.
[00:08:12] Evan: Does Redwood support automatic graph eviction/aging if shapes change?
[00:08:17] Maya: Yes, our runtime has a graph cache with LRU policies and shape-bucketing. We also expose hooks for you to pin graphs for critical shapes. However, if your shape cardinality is high, memory pressure will force evictions.
[00:08:34] Jordan: Another nuance — kernel selection: the runtime auto-selects between multiple kernel implementations (cutlass, custom fused kernels, TensorRT fused kernels). We log the decisions in the trace; Maya can point to the trace fields.
[00:08:49] Maya: In our traces you'll see fields like chosen_kernel:trt_fused_v2 or cutlass_split; they map to perf delta. We'll share a decoder for the trace fields.
[00:09:02] Priya: We'll need those traces to debug a case where p99 jumps intermittently.
[00:09:07] Maya: We'll attach a sample trace. It's in the perf zip: perf-traces/arcadia-20260815.tar.gz (link).
[00:09:18] Dr. Sara: Regarding VPC/on-prem: What are the ops that leak metadata or require special networking to your control plane?
[00:09:26] Liam: For Redwood Private, the control plane is optional; you can run completely offline with our on-prem package. For metrics and traces we can integrate with your internal telemetry; nothing leaves your VPC unless you opt in. For KMS, we support bringing your own key and HSM integrations.
[00:09:44] Marcus: Good. For audit we'll need detailed call logs and access logs for model events.
[00:09:49] Jordan: We can enable long retention on logs and provide signed attestations.
[00:09:54] Priya: Back to perf: are there any immediate config changes we can make to reduce p99 right now?
[00:10:00] Maya: Short-term: (1) pin a small warm pool of TRT-LLM instances for your top 5 frequent shapes, (2) enable prefix/KV caching for chat sessions to avoid full recompute, (3) route critical interactive traffic to FP16 instances pinned to GPU. Medium-term: run mixed-precision/INT8 evals on your prompts and, if acceptable, deploy mixed quant kernels.
[00:10:28] Evan: Sounds actionable. For the warm pool, how many instances?
[00:10:31] Maya: Depends on concurrency — for 100 RPS of short chats I'd start with 4-8 pinned instances. We'll model this in the cost estimate.
[00:10:42] [00:10:42] Jordan: Let's capture next steps — I'll list and Maya will own the technical bench runs.
[00:10:48] Jordan: Next steps: 1) Redwood to run a targeted benchmark (short/medium/long mix) on Arcadia's representative prompts using TRT-LLM and vLLM and include CUDA graph warm/cold runs. 2) Arcadia to share a redacted prompt set + expected SLOs. 3) Redwood to provide kernel selection trace decoder and perf traces. 4) Schedule a follow-up to review results and pilot plan.
[00:11:12] Priya: We'll share prompts by EOD Monday.
[00:11:16] Evan: We also want a rough cost estimate for pinned warm pool vs burst capacity.
[00:11:20] Jordan: We'll include that in the benchmark report.
[00:11:24] Dr. Sara: One more Q — how do you measure correctness/regressions for quantization?
[00:11:29] Maya: We run eval suites on your prompt/eval set and report metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/EM) and also run token-level diff and hallucination checks. We'll surface samples that regress and suggest layer-level adjustments.
[00:11:46] Marcus: For our compliance team, can you provide SOC2 artifacts and a diagram of network flows for private deployment?
[00:11:52] Jordan: Yes — I'll attach the SOC2 summary and a network architecture diagram for the Private offering.
[00:11:58] Priya: Any gotchas for NVIDIA driver versions or CUDA compatibility?
[00:12:03] Maya: Use CUDA 12.x and the driver versions we list in the on-prem requirements. Some TensorRT fused kernels require very specific minor versions. We'll provide an ops checklist.
[00:12:15] Evan: Cool.
[00:12:18] [00:12:18] Jordan: Action items and owners we'll capture in the CRM. Anything else before we wrap?
[00:12:25] Dr. Sara: Not from us. Thanks — that was very useful.
[00:12:29] Jordan: Great, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and perf sheet.
[00:12:34] Maya: And I'll send the trace decoder and a sample perf trace.
[00:12:39] Evan: Thanks everyone.
[00:12:42] [end of recorded transcript — meeting continued offline for 45 mins of Q/A and live profiling; additional notes uploaded separately],
